teaser: A guardian with a king's beard, an eagle's wings and one leg too many.
review_notes:
The Met dates the figure about 883-859 BC (reign of Ashurnasirpal II); the catalog year -870 is an approximation.
Height about 3.1 m and material (gypsum alabaster): from the Met.
Provenance: excavated by Layard, kept at Canford Manor in England, bought by John D. Rockefeller Jr. and given to the Met in 1932: check.
Banquet of 69,574 guests: from Ashurnasirpal's Banquet Stele.
Destruction of lamassu at Nimrud and Nineveh in 2015: check.
The knotted belt and the inscription between the legs are faint in this photo; spots were placed where they appear in the image.
The 'fifth leg' is identified as the striding foreleg seen in the middle of the side view.

lesson.text: How many legs does a lion have? Hold on to your answer. You are about to meet one, carved almost three thousand years ago for a king's doorway, and it is going to disagree with you.

It stands about 3.1 meters tall (just over 10 feet), cut from a single slab of gypsum alabaster, a soft gray stone found near the Tigris river. Around 870 BC it guarded a gateway in the palace of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud, in the north of what is now Iraq. Anyone going in to see the king had to walk past it.

The Assyrians called such a creature a lamassu: a protective spirit, built from the strongest parts they knew. A man's head for intelligence, a lion's body for power, a bird's wings for speed. The photo shows it from the front corner, the angle at which a visitor would first have seen it.
Now count. One of these legs should not be there. Which one?

spots.title: The fifth leg
spots.text: Two front legs stand side by side at the corner. Two hind legs walk at the back. This one, stepping forward in the middle, is an extra foreleg that only makes sense from the side.

lesson.text: Five legs, and the reason is the doorway. Seen from the front as you approached, the lion stands firm on two legs, at attention. Seen from the side as you passed through, four legs stride along with you. The sculptor carved both views into one block and accepted an impossible animal as the result.
The lamassu is designed for a person in motion. It stands still when you face it and walks when you walk.

When Ashurnasirpal finished his new capital, he gave a party. An inscription of his claims 69,574 guests, fed for ten days on thousands of sheep, oxen, birds and fish, with ten thousand skins of wine.

This is not quite a statue. The back half is still attached to its slab, a kind of carving called relief, where forms rise from a flat background. Only the head and chest come fully free of the stone, pushing out into the visitor's space.
Start at the top, where the creature tells you what it is.

spots.title: The horned cap
spots.text: A tall rounded cap with pairs of horns curving up its sides. In Mesopotamia only gods and spirits wear horns, so this headgear marks the creature as divine.

spots.title: The beard
spots.text: Rows of tight curls, then long waves, then curls again, ending square. It is the formal beard of Assyrian kings and courtiers, each lock cut like a pattern.

spots.title: A human ear
spots.text: Lions on other reliefs keep their animal ears. This one has a man's ear, complete with a long earring.

spots.title: The wing
spots.text: Three ranks of feathers sweep back across the slab. Each feather has a central rib and fine barbs scratched in with a pointed tool.

lesson.title: Reading the monster

lesson.text: The face is calm, almost kind, with wide eyes under one continuous brow. Guardians in many cultures snarl. This one simply watches, and its size does the rest. The stone was once brighter too: Assyrian carvings carried paint, and traces of color have been found on figures like this.

Between the legs, where the background is flat, the surface is covered with a fine regular texture. That is writing. The king had the same text cut on slab after slab of his palace in cuneiform, a script made of small wedge-shaped marks pressed or carved in rows.
The text is known as the Standard Inscription. It lists the king's titles and ancestors, boasts of his conquests and describes the building of the palace. It was repeated on hundreds of slabs.

The palace burned when the Assyrian empire fell in 612 BC, and the mud-brick walls collapsed over the stone guardians. They stayed buried until the 1840s, when the English explorer Austen Henry Layard dug into the mound at Nimrud and found bearded heads rising out of the earth.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Large almond eyes, a strong nose, a small closed mouth. The same face, with the same expression, appears on the king's human attendants.

spots.title: The hair
spots.text: Behind the ear the hair falls to the shoulder and ends in a thick bunch of spiral curls.

spots.title: The chest
spots.text: Overlapping scale shapes cover the breast like feathers or a mane. Lion, bird and man blend here with no visible seam.

spots.title: The belt
spots.text: A cord circles the lion's body and its tasseled end hangs on the flank. The museum reads this belt as a sign of the creature's power.

spots.title: The front paws
spots.text: Broad lion paws with every claw and knuckle marked, planted on the base at the corner of the block.

spots.title: The tail tip
spots.text: The tail drops straight down behind the hind legs and ends in a round tuft, just above the base.

spots.title: The writing
spots.text: Fine wedge-shaped signs fill the flat stone between the legs. From a distance they look like a texture.

lesson.text: Getting it to New York took most of a century. Layard's finds went to England, where this lion and its partner, a winged bull, decorated a country house. John D. Rockefeller Jr. bought them and gave them to the Metropolitan Museum in 1932.

In 2015, militants filmed themselves smashing lamassu that still stood in Iraq, at Nimrud and at a gate of ancient Nineveh. The ones that had left for museums are now among the best preserved. It is an uncomfortable fact, and it is part of what you see when you look at this one: a guardian that outlasted the place it was made to protect.

quiz.question: Why does the lamassu have five legs?
options: So it looks correct from both the front and the side
quiz.explanation: Two legs show from the front, four from the side, sharing the corner leg.

quiz.question: What marks the creature as divine?
quiz.explanation: In Mesopotamia horns on headgear belong to gods and spirits.

quiz.question: Where did it originally stand?
options: In a palace gateway at Nimrud
quiz.explanation: It guarded a doorway of Ashurnasirpal II's palace.

quiz.question: What is cuneiform?
options: A carving that stands free of its background
quiz.explanation: The inscription between the legs is in this wedge-shaped script.

quiz.question: Who excavated the palace at Nimrud in the 1840s?
quiz.explanation: Layard dug into the mound and found the buried guardians.

facts.text: The lamassu was carved from a single slab of stone.
facts.explanation: It is one block of gypsum alabaster about 3.1 meters tall.

facts.text: The creature is shown snarling to frighten visitors.
facts.explanation: Its face is calm with a closed mouth.

facts.text: The whole figure stands free of the stone, like a statue in the round.
facts.explanation: The back half is relief, still attached to its slab.
